opus-5.5.text:
I think research taste is almost the whole ballgame, honestly. People sometimes imagine automated discovery as this brute-force thing: you spin up a million agents, they try a million ideas, and you just filter for what works. But the search space in any interesting research domain is so astronomically large that you can't enumerate your way through it. The bottleneck isn't the ability to run experiments, it's knowing which experiments are worth running in the first place.

When I think about what taste actually is, I'd describe it as a learned prior over what's going to be interesting and tractable. A good researcher looks at a problem and has this intuition: "this direction smells like it'll compound," or "this is a dead end that looks shiny." That intuition is built from years of seeing which ideas panned out and which didn't, and a lot of it is implicit. It's hard to articulate, which is exactly why it's hard to automate.

What's interesting is that I think taste is learnable in the machine learning sense. It's essentially a value function. If you frame research as a sequential decision problem, choosing a question, designing an experiment, interpreting a result, deciding what to try next, then taste is your estimate of the long-horizon value of each of those choices. The challenge is that the reward signal is incredibly sparse and delayed. You might not know whether a research direction was good for years. So the credit assignment problem is brutal.

That said, I'm optimistic about a couple of things. One is that models trained on the enormous corpus of scientific literature have already absorbed a decent amount of implicit taste. They've seen which papers got cited, which ideas got built upon, how fields evolved. That's a weak but real signal. The other is that in domains where you can close the loop quickly, say certain kinds of ML experiments, or areas of math with formal verification, you can actually get enough feedback to start refining that value function through something like reinforcement learning.

I'd also say taste isn't just about picking good problems; it's about knowing when to stop. A lot of research waste comes from pushing on something past the point where the evidence says it's not working, or abandoning something too early because the first experiment was noisy. Calibrating that is a big part of what separates great researchers from good ones, and I think it's going to be one of the harder things to get right for automated systems.

So my view is: compute and experimentation throughput are necessary but not sufficient. The thing that makes automated discovery tractable rather than just expensive is getting the taste, the prioritization, the value function, good enough that you're searching in the right neighborhood. And the nice thing is that once you have even a modestly good version of that, it can improve itself, because better taste leads to better experiments, which gives you better data to refine your taste.

fable-5.1.text:
I think taste is doing a lot more of the work than people want to admit, and the reason it matters for automation is that it's the part we understand least.

When people picture automated discovery, they imagine the bottleneck is the loop: propose a hypothesis, run the experiment, read the result, update, repeat. And sure, you can get a model to do that loop today. The problem is that the search space is enormous and almost every direction in it is boring. The thing a good researcher has isn't more throughput through the loop, it's a prior over which ten experiments out of ten thousand are actually worth running. That prior is what we call taste.

The weird part is that taste is mostly built from failure. You spend years running things that don't work, and you end up with this compressed, kind of inarticulate sense of "that idea smells wrong" or "that result is too clean, something's leaking." Nobody writes that down. It isn't in the papers, because papers are the survivorship-biased tail. So when you train on the literature, you get the outputs of taste without the process that produced it.

So my honest answer is: taste is what makes discovery tractable at all, for humans or machines, because it's the thing that collapses the search space. And the open question for automation isn't "can the model run experiments," it's "can the model develop a prior from its own failed experiments faster than we can." If it can, you get something that compounds. If it can't, you just get a very fast grad student who tries everything, and that's expensive and mostly useless.

I'd also push back a little on treating taste as mystical. I think a lot of it is just calibration. Good researchers are well-calibrated about what the next result will be, so they're surprised less often, and they chase the things that do surprise them. That's actually a learnable thing. You could imagine an agent that keeps a running prediction before every experiment and explicitly tracks where it's wrong. That's not elegant, but I suspect something like that is how you bootstrap taste rather than hoping it emerges from scale.

astra-6.text:
I think research taste is largely about deciding which experiments are worth running. The space of things you could try is enormous, and most of them won’t teach you very much. So even if you automate the mechanics of research, you still need some way to allocate your compute toward promising questions.

And promising doesn’t necessarily mean an experiment is likely to succeed. Sometimes you want an experiment that distinguishes between two explanations. A negative result can be incredibly useful if it tells you which direction to stop pursuing. That’s a harder objective than just asking, “Did the benchmark number go up?”

My intuition is that taste is something you can learn. You propose things, see what happens, and develop better intuitions about what’s worth trying. The challenge for automated discovery is making that feedback loop work over longer horizons, where an idea might look unproductive initially but eventually open up a whole new direction.

sol-6.1.text:
I think research taste is partly about knowing which experiments are worth running, but it’s also about choosing a representation where the problem becomes tractable. You can search over an enormous space of possibilities, but if you’re searching in the wrong space, more compute doesn’t necessarily get you very far.

A researcher with good taste might say, “This result looks bad, but the failure is interesting. It suggests we should change this assumption.” Or, “This benchmark looks impressive, but it doesn’t actually tell us whether the underlying idea works.” Those judgments determine where you spend your next unit of effort.

For automated discovery, the question is whether you can close that loop: propose an experiment, run it, interpret the result, and decide what to do next. If you have a cheap, reliable evaluator, you can substitute a lot of search for taste. But in research, figuring out what to evaluate is often part of the problem. So I think taste is especially valuable where the feedback is ambiguous—and automating that judgment is a much bigger challenge than just generating more hypotheses.
